MW groups citr- with longer forms. Independently, Collins explicitly lists citr- as the pre-vowel variant for citrus/citrus fruits, and Dictionary.com gives citric from citr(us)+-ic. Exact surface and source sense are substantiated, with the independently valid citrus + -ic derivational history and alternative citri- grouping carefully kept separate. Dictionary.com categorizes citric as chemistry; the familiar food-label expression citric acid supplies general cultural value, but the word is not a synonym for an actual citrus fruit and its meaning depends on context. Accept source sense 1 citrus as demonstrated by this example. The source also lists citric acid and citrate as additional distinct senses, with different source examples; preserve them as separate pending meanings unless each is independently supported. Do not merge all three as equally demonstrated by citric. Avoid treating the i as belonging exclusively to both citri- and -ic at once.

More robustly, Partridge Origins, entry laurel, explicitly identifies Latin laurus stem laur- and lists laureate in its family. Etymonline traces Latin laureatus through laurea crown and laureus to laurus. The short form is a documented historical teaching stem, not a claim that English directly coined laureate as laur + eate. The modern award-recipient sense reflects honor rather than literal crowning. Accept laurel sense only for laureate; keep lauric-acid chemical sense separately pending until supported with its own exact example. Describe historical derivation and separate present sense.
